items.readable_text:
Content:
Just as we can have a system of linear equations, we can also have systems of linear inequalities. For example, the system

Content:
[MATH: y ≤ x + 2; y > − x]
is solved by the points that satisfy the inequalities [MATH: y \leq x+2] and [MATH: y>-x] simultaneously.

Content:
To find the points that satisfy both inequalities, we first draw the graph of the inequality [MATH: y \leq x + 2{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0118424e31e628629f7e60b87611205d]

Content:
Now, on top of the diagram above, we draw the graph of the second inequality, [MATH: y > -x{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d5c85a9c4ff25953ac92b95b406874bd]

Content:
The solution to the system is the intersection of the two regions (i.e., the part that is shaded twice).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b59080e9a4cf84e74344a6251f7c0e99]

Content:
The important thing to realize is that any point in the shaded region above satisfies both inequalities.

sections.readable_text:

Which system of inequalities defines the shaded region shown above?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the line [MATH: y = 2x - 1.] Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies below the line, the inequality is a "less than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is [MATH: y \leq 2x - 1.]

Now consider the line [MATH: y = -x+2.] Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies above the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is [MATH: y \geq -x + 2.]

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines our shaded region is [MATH: {y ≤ 2x − 1; y ≥ − x + 2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the line [MATH: y=1.] Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict. Also, since the shaded region lies below the line, the inequality is a "less than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is [MATH: y < 1.]

Now consider the line [MATH: x - y = 2.] Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Writing the equation of this line in slope-intercept form, we have [MATH: y =x- 2.]

Now, since the shaded region lies above the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is [MATH: y \geq x - 2,] which we can rewrite as [MATH: x-y \leq 2.] Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

[MATH: {y < 1; x − y ≤ 2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Just as we can have a system of linear equations, we can also have systems of linear inequalities. For example, the system

Content:
[MATH: y ≤ x + 2; y > − x]
is solved by the points that satisfy the inequalities [MATH: y \leq x+2] and [MATH: y>-x] simultaneously.

Content:
To find the points that satisfy both inequalities, we first draw the graph of the inequality [MATH: y \leq x + 2{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0118424e31e628629f7e60b87611205d]

Content:
Now, on top of the diagram above, we draw the graph of the second inequality, [MATH: y > -x{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d5c85a9c4ff25953ac92b95b406874bd]

Content:
The solution to the system is the intersection of the two regions (i.e., the part that is shaded twice).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b59080e9a4cf84e74344a6251f7c0e99]

Content:
The important thing to realize is that any point in the shaded region above satisfies both inequalities.

---

Item 2 — Example: Working With Systems Containing "Or Equal To" Inequalities

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/3edbb889f6978133fc2ae041a3085a33]

Which system of inequalities defines the shaded region shown above?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Consider the line [MATH: y = 2x - 1.] Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies below the line, the inequality is a "less than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is
[MATH: y \leq 2x - 1.]

Now consider the line [MATH: y = -x+2.] Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies above the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is
[MATH: y \geq -x + 2.]

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines our shaded region is
[MATH: {y ≤ 2x − 1; y ≥ − x + 2.]
